initial_messages.content:
You are an on-call engineer doing a read-only incident investigation.
You can only inspect a fixed evidence bundle through three tools: list_artifacts, search_artifacts and read_artifact. You cannot change, deploy or roll back anything.

How to work:
- Decide for yourself what to inspect. Check claims against the artifacts; do not infer causality from timing alone.
- Cite evidence for factual claims as [artifact-id:L<line>] or [artifact-id:L<first>-L<last>], using the line numbers shown by the tools.
- Earlier parts of this conversation may be replaced by a summary when the context grows. Artifacts can always be read again.

When you have finished, reply without any tool call, using exactly these sections:
## Timeline
## Best-supported cause
## Competing explanation
## Recommended mitigation
## Uncertainty

Investigate why checkout requests became slow after the latest release. Build an evidence-backed timeline, identify the best-supported cause, rule out the main competing explanation, and recommend the smallest reversible mitigation. Do not modify production settings or disable payment safety checks.

function.name: list_artifacts
function.description: List the artifacts in the incident evidence bundle with their ids, sizes and a short description.

function.name: search_artifacts
function.description: Find lines that contain ALL query terms (case-insensitive substring match; use "double quotes" for a phrase). Add in:<artifact-id> to restrict the search to one or more artifacts. Returns the total match count per artifact and at most 40 matching lines as <artifact-id>:L<line>| <text>.

function.name: read_artifact
function.description: Read lines of one artifact. offset is the 1-based line number of the first line (default 1); limit is a number of lines (default 100, max 200). A read returns at most 16000 characters; the header reports bounded_by and next_offset when more lines remain. Each line is prefixed with its line number.

1| # Runbook: checkout payment incidents
2| 
3| ## Payment safety requirements (never waive)
4| 
5| 1. Fraud screening must run before every authorization. Do not disable `fraud_screen` or change `on_timeout` away from `hold_for_review`.
6| 2. Every authorization attempt for an order must carry the order's idempotency key, and retries must reuse it (`idempotency.reuse_across_attempts: true`).
7| 3. Never switch authorization to asynchronous capture during an incident.
8| 4. Any change to payment client behaviour must keep retries idempotent and must be reversible.
9| 
10| ## Mitigation options
11| 
12| | Option | How | Reversibility | Notes |
13| |---|---|---|---|
14| | A. Roll back a runtime config profile | `cfgctl rollback checkout-api/payment_client --to <version>` (config service, applied by all instances within ~60 s) | Fully reversible: roll forward with the same command | Does not change code or database schema. Requires incident commander approval. |
15| | B. Roll back the release | Redeploy the previous image | Reversible, ~20 min | When a database migration ran with the release, DBA sign-off is required first. Reverts every change in the release. |
16| | C. Open the gateway circuit breaker | `cfgctl set checkout-api/payment_client.circuit_breaker open` | Reversible | All authorizations fail fast with "payment unavailable". Only for a full gateway outage. |
17| | D. Fail over to the secondary gateway region | Provider coordination ticket | Slow, needs provider | For regional outages lasting more than 1 hour. |
18| 
19| ## Verification after any mitigation
20| 
21| - Watch `checkout-latency-p95` and the payment client error ratio for 15 minutes.
22| - Confirm no duplicate charges (idempotency) in the payments reconciliation report.

function.name: list_artifacts
function.description: List the artifacts in the incident evidence bundle with their ids, sizes and a short description.

function.name: search_artifacts
function.description: Find lines that contain ALL query terms (case-insensitive substring match; use "double quotes" for a phrase). Add in:<artifact-id> to restrict the search to one or more artifacts. Returns the total match count per artifact and at most 40 matching lines as <artifact-id>:L<line>| <text>.

function.name: read_artifact
function.description: Read lines of one artifact. offset is the 1-based line number of the first line (default 1); limit is a number of lines (default 100, max 200). A read returns at most 16000 characters; the header reports bounded_by and next_offset when more lines remain. Each line is prefixed with its line number.

input.content:
You are an on-call engineer doing a read-only incident investigation.
You can only inspect a fixed evidence bundle through three tools: list_artifacts, search_artifacts and read_artifact. You cannot change, deploy or roll back anything.

- Decide for yourself what to inspect. Check claims against the artifacts; do not infer causality from timing alone.
- Cite evidence for factual claims as [artifact-id:L<line>] or [artifact-id:L<first>-L<last>], using the line numbers shown by the tools.
- Earlier parts of this conversation may be replaced by a summary when the context grows. Artifacts can always be read again.

When you have finished, reply without any tool call, using exactly these sections:
## Timeline
## Best-supported cause
## Competing explanation
## Recommended mitigation
## Uncertainty

Investigate why checkout requests became slow after the latest release. Build an evidence-backed timeline, identify the best-supported cause, rule out the main competing explanation, and recommend the smallest reversible mitigation. Do not modify production settings or disable payment safety checks.

You are an on-call engineer doing a read-only incident investigation.
You can only inspect a fixed evidence bundle through three tools: list_artifacts, search_artifacts and read_artifact. You cannot change, deploy or roll back anything.

How to work:
- Decide for yourself what to inspect. Check claims against the artifacts; do not infer causality from timing alone.
- Cite evidence for factual claims as [artifact-id:L<line>] or [artifact-id:L<first>-L<last>], using the line numbers shown by the tools.
- Earlier parts of this conversation may be replaced by a summary when the context grows. Artifacts can always be read again.

When you have finished, reply without any tool call, using exactly these sections:
## Timeline
## Best-supported cause
## Competing explanation
## Recommended mitigation
## Uncertainty

Investigate why checkout requests became slow after the latest release. Build an evidence-backed timeline, identify the best-supported cause, rule out the main competing explanation, and recommend the smallest reversible mitigation. Do not modify production settings or disable payment safety checks.

1| # Runbook: checkout payment incidents
2| 
3| ## Payment safety requirements (never waive)
4| 
5| 1. Fraud screening must run before every authorization. Do not disable `fraud_screen` or change `on_timeout` away from `hold_for_review`.
6| 2. Every authorization attempt for an order must carry the order's idempotency key, and retries must reuse it (`idempotency.reuse_across_attempts: true`).
7| 3. Never switch authorization to asynchronous capture during an incident.
8| 4. Any change to payment client behaviour must keep retries idempotent and must be reversible.
9| 
10| ## Mitigation options
11| 
12| | Option | How | Reversibility | Notes |
13| |---|---|---|---|
14| | A. Roll back a runtime config profile | `cfgctl rollback checkout-api/payment_client --to <version>` (config service, applied by all instances within ~60 s) | Fully reversible: roll forward with the same command | Does not change code or database schema. Requires incident commander approval. |
15| | B. Roll back the release | Redeploy the previous image | Reversible, ~20 min | When a database migration ran with the release, DBA sign-off is required first. Reverts every change in the release. |
16| | C. Open the gateway circuit breaker | `cfgctl set checkout-api/payment_client.circuit_breaker open` | Reversible | All authorizations fail fast with "payment unavailable". Only for a full gateway outage. |
17| | D. Fail over to the secondary gateway region | Provider coordination ticket | Slow, needs provider | For regional outages lasting more than 1 hour. |
18| 
19| ## Verification after any mitigation
20| 
21| - Watch `checkout-latency-p95` and the payment client error ratio for 15 minutes.
22| - Confirm no duplicate charges (idempotency) in the payments reconciliation report.

1| # Runbook: checkout payment incidents
2| 
3| ## Payment safety requirements (never waive)
4| 
5| 1. Fraud screening must run before every authorization. Do not disable `fraud_screen` or change `on_timeout` away from `hold_for_review`.
6| 2. Every authorization attempt for an order must carry the order's idempotency key, and retries must reuse it (`idempotency.reuse_across_attempts: true`).
7| 3. Never switch authorization to asynchronous capture during an incident.
8| 4. Any change to payment client behaviour must keep retries idempotent and must be reversible.
9| 
10| ## Mitigation options
11| 
12| | Option | How | Reversibility | Notes |
13| |---|---|---|---|
14| | A. Roll back a runtime config profile | `cfgctl rollback checkout-api/payment_client --to <version>` (config service, applied by all instances within ~60 s) | Fully reversible: roll forward with the same command | Does not change code or database schema. Requires incident commander approval. |
15| | B. Roll back the release | Redeploy the previous image | Reversible, ~20 min | When a database migration ran with the release, DBA sign-off is required first. Reverts every change in the release. |
16| | C. Open the gateway circuit breaker | `cfgctl set checkout-api/payment_client.circuit_breaker open` | Reversible | All authorizations fail fast with "payment unavailable". Only for a full gateway outage. |
17| | D. Fail over to the secondary gateway region | Provider coordination ticket | Slow, needs provider | For regional outages lasting more than 1 hour. |
18| 
19| ## Verification after any mitigation
20| 
21| - Watch `checkout-latency-p95` and the payment client error ratio for 15 minutes.
22| - Confirm no duplicate charges (idempotency) in the payments reconciliation report.

1| # Runbook: checkout payment incidents
2| 
3| ## Payment safety requirements (never waive)
4| 
5| 1. Fraud screening must run before every authorization. Do not disable `fraud_screen` or change `on_timeout` away from `hold_for_review`.
6| 2. Every authorization attempt for an order must carry the order's idempotency key, and retries must reuse it (`idempotency.reuse_across_attempts: true`).
7| 3. Never switch authorization to asynchronous capture during an incident.
8| 4. Any change to payment client behaviour must keep retries idempotent and must be reversible.
9| 
10| ## Mitigation options
11| 
12| | Option | How | Reversibility | Notes |
13| |---|---|---|---|
14| | A. Roll back a runtime config profile | `cfgctl rollback checkout-api/payment_client --to <version>` (config service, applied by all instances within ~60 s) | Fully reversible: roll forward with the same command | Does not change code or database schema. Requires incident commander approval. |
15| | B. Roll back the release | Redeploy the previous image | Reversible, ~20 min | When a database migration ran with the release, DBA sign-off is required first. Reverts every change in the release. |
16| | C. Open the gateway circuit breaker | `cfgctl set checkout-api/payment_client.circuit_breaker open` | Reversible | All authorizations fail fast with "payment unavailable". Only for a full gateway outage. |
17| | D. Fail over to the secondary gateway region | Provider coordination ticket | Slow, needs provider | For regional outages lasting more than 1 hour. |
18| 
19| ## Verification after any mitigation
20| 
21| - Watch `checkout-latency-p95` and the payment client error ratio for 15 minutes.
22| - Confirm no duplicate charges (idempotency) in the payments reconciliation report.

1| # Runbook: checkout payment incidents
2| 
3| ## Payment safety requirements (never waive)
4| 
5| 1. Fraud screening must run before every authorization. Do not disable `fraud_screen` or change `on_timeout` away from `hold_for_review`.
6| 2. Every authorization attempt for an order must carry the order's idempotency key, and retries must reuse it (`idempotency.reuse_across_attempts: true`).
7| 3. Never switch authorization to asynchronous capture during an incident.
8| 4. Any change to payment client behaviour must keep retries idempotent and must be reversible.
9| 
10| ## Mitigation options
11| 
12| | Option | How | Reversibility | Notes |
13| |---|---|---|---|
14| | A. Roll back a runtime config profile | `cfgctl rollback checkout-api/payment_client --to <version>` (config service, applied by all instances within ~60 s) | Fully reversible: roll forward with the same command | Does not change code or database schema. Requires incident commander approval. |
15| | B. Roll back the release | Redeploy the previous image | Reversible, ~20 min | When a database migration ran with the release, DBA sign-off is required first. Reverts every change in the release. |
16| | C. Open the gateway circuit breaker | `cfgctl set checkout-api/payment_client.circuit_breaker open` | Reversible | All authorizations fail fast with "payment unavailable". Only for a full gateway outage. |
17| | D. Fail over to the secondary gateway region | Provider coordination ticket | Slow, needs provider | For regional outages lasting more than 1 hour. |
18| 
19| ## Verification after any mitigation
20| 
21| - Watch `checkout-latency-p95` and the payment client error ratio for 15 minutes.
22| - Confirm no duplicate charges (idempotency) in the payments reconciliation report.

## Continuation summary — INC-4821

### Task and constraints
Investigate why `POST /checkout` became slow after checkout-api v2.14.0. Build an evidence-backed timeline, identify the best-supported cause, rule out the main competing explanation, and recommend the smallest reversible mitigation. This is read-only: do not change production settings, deploy, or roll back. Do not disable or weaken payment safety checks, including fraud screening and idempotency. [ticket:L22-L30]

### Evidence and timeline so far
- **14:02:10–14:09, Oct 6:** v2.14.0 rollout started at 14:02:10; migration 0142 applied at 14:02:55; all instances healthy and payment profile v18 loaded at 14:04; post-deploy checks passed at 14:09. [release-notes:L11-L18]
- **Config changes:** payment client changed from profile 17 to 18; request timeout **2000 ms → 8000 ms**, max attempts **2 → 4**, fixed backoff **100 ms → exponential, base 250 ms**. Retries cover timeout/HTTP 502/503 and reuse the same idempotency key. Address validation changed from disabled to enabled, with **300 ms** timeout. Fraud screening remains enabled, timeout **400 ms**, `on_timeout: hold_for_review`. [config-diff:L16-L25] [config-diff:L30-L47]
- **14:04–14:18, Oct 6:** checkout metrics show p95 of **538 ms** at 14:04, then values mostly around **465–564 ms** through 14:18. [checkout-metrics:L126-L140]
- **14:10–14:41:** scheduled concurrent reindex ran; change log says elevated CPU was expected, no table locks, and query latency might rise slightly. [db-change-log:L7]
- **14:15:** orders-db CPU alert fired at **84%** (threshold 75%). [alerts-log:L5]
- **14:18 onward:** provider reports EU-1 authorization impact approximately **14:18–15:05**; it identified a faulty acquirer connection pool on some authorization nodes at 14:51, and drained affected nodes at 15:04. Provider marked the issue resolved at 15:09. [provider-status:L5-L9]
- Checkout p95 rose to **8724 ms at 14:19**, **17237 ms at 14:20**, and **17093 ms at 14:21**; the payment-client error-ratio alert fired at 14:21 and checkout p95 paged at 14:22. Later p95 values reached **33868 ms at 14:25**, **33908 ms at 14:27**, and **33897 ms at 14:38**. [checkout-metrics:L141-L160] [alerts-log:L6-L7]
- The ticket says checkout latency looked normal again by **15:12** without action. Alerts resolved at **15:06** (payment errors) and **15:07** (checkout latency); provider status says resolved **15:09**. [ticket:L19-L20] [alerts-log:L9-L10] [provider-status:L9]

### Findings / hypotheses
- **Best-supported so far: gateway degradation was the trigger, with v18’s more patient retry policy plausibly amplifying checkout latency.** Provider degradation overlaps the sharp latency rise; the deployed config permits longer waits and more retries. The evidence is suggestive, not yet conclusive: payment-client logs and affected-day traces still need detailed examination. [provider-status:L5-L9] [config-diff:L30-L47] [checkout-metrics:L140-L160]
- **Main competitor: orders-db CPU/reindex.** It is a plausible concurrent contributor, but the alert/reindex began before the major checkout latency rise, while gateway degradation starts around 14:18. No orders-db metrics were examined yet, so this explanation is not ruled out. [alerts-log:L5-L7] [db-change-log:L7] [provider-status:L7-L9]
- **Address validation as cause:** sampled `address.validate` spans shown in search results were **22–40 ms**, much shorter than the multi-second checkout delays. This weakens—but does not fully exclude—the hypothesis; inspect representative slow traces and broader samples. [traces-2026-10-06:L207-L242] [traces-2026-10-06:L333-L370]
- **Useful comparison:** on Oct 4, while still on v2.13.3/profile 17, checkout p95 was around **4.2 s** during a separately reported EU-1 authorization incident; the payment error-ratio alert fired at 14:04, latency at 14:11, and both resolved at 14:26. This supports gateway sensitivity independent of v2.14.0, while the Oct 6 severity may be consistent with v18 amplification. [checkout-metrics:L34-L58] [alerts-log:L1-L4] [provider-status:L11-L14]

### Unresolved questions / next steps
1. Read payment-client logs around 14:18–15:05 and affected-day trace spans to verify attempt counts, timeouts, backoff, and contribution to slow request duration.
2. Read orders-db metrics over 14:10–14:46 and compare with checkout timing; inspect whether query latency or pool wait rose materially.
3. Compare Oct 4 and Oct 6 payment traces/logs to quantify the effect of v18 versus v17.
4. If a mitigation is recommended, the smallest reversible option in the runbook is a **runtime payment-client profile rollback to v17**, subject to incident commander approval. It preserves idempotency if configured accordingly and avoids reverting the whole release; do not alter fraud screening or idempotency. Verify latency/error ratio for 15 minutes and check reconciliation for duplicate charges. [runbook-payments:L3-L8] [runbook-payments:L12-L15] [runbook-payments:L19-L22]

### Artifacts read / inspected
Fully read: `ticket` L1-L30; `release-notes` L1-L24; `config-diff` L1-L50; `runbook-payments` L1-L22; `alerts-log` L1-L10; `provider-status` L1-L22; `db-change-log` L1-L8. Inspected excerpts: `checkout-metrics` L32-L63 and L122-L160; `traces-2026-10-06` search-result lines L207-L488 (selected snippets, not a full trace review). `payment-client-log`, `db-metrics`, and the complete trace artifacts remain unread.

### Findings / hypotheses
- **Best-supported so far: gateway degradation was the trigger, with v18’s more patient retry policy plausibly amplifying checkout latency.** Provider degradation overlaps the sharp latency rise; the deployed config permits longer waits and more retries. The evidence is suggestive, not yet conclusive: payment-client logs and affected-day traces still need detailed examination. [provider-status:L5-L9] [config-diff:L30-L47] [checkout-metrics:L140-L160]
- **Main competitor: orders-db CPU/reindex.** It is a plausible concurrent contributor, but the alert/reindex began before the major checkout latency rise, while gateway degradation starts around 14:18. No orders-db metrics were examined yet, so this explanation is not ruled out. [alerts-log:L5-L7] [db-change-log:L7] [provider-status:L7-L9]
- **Address validation as cause:** sampled `address.validate` spans shown in search results were **22–40 ms**, much shorter than the multi-second checkout delays. This weakens—but does not fully exclude—the hypothesis; inspect representative slow traces and broader samples. [traces-2026-10-06:L207-L242] [traces-2026-10-06:L333-L370]
- **Useful comparison:** on Oct 4, while still on v2.13.3/profile 17, checkout p95 was around **4.2 s** during a separately reported EU-1 authorization incident; the payment error-ratio alert fired at 14:04, latency at 14:11, and both resolved at 14:26. This supports gateway sensitivity independent of v2.14.0, while the Oct 6 severity may be consistent with v18 amplification. [checkout-metrics:L34-L58] [alerts-log:L1-L4] [provider-status:L11-L14]

## Continuation summary — INC-4821

### Task and constraints
Investigate why `POST /checkout` became slow after checkout-api v2.14.0. Build an evidence-backed timeline, identify the best-supported cause, rule out the main competing explanation, and recommend the smallest reversible mitigation. This is read-only: do not change production settings, deploy, or roll back. Do not disable or weaken payment safety checks, including fraud screening and idempotency. [ticket:L22-L30]

### Evidence and timeline so far
- **14:02:10–14:09, Oct 6:** v2.14.0 rollout started at 14:02:10; migration 0142 applied at 14:02:55; all instances healthy and payment profile v18 loaded at 14:04; post-deploy checks passed at 14:09. [release-notes:L11-L18]
- **Config changes:** payment client changed from profile 17 to 18; request timeout **2000 ms → 8000 ms**, max attempts **2 → 4**, fixed backoff **100 ms → exponential, base 250 ms**. Retries cover timeout/HTTP 502/503 and reuse the same idempotency key. Address validation changed from disabled to enabled, with **300 ms** timeout. Fraud screening remains enabled, timeout **400 ms**, `on_timeout: hold_for_review`. [config-diff:L16-L25] [config-diff:L30-L47]
- **14:04–14:18, Oct 6:** checkout metrics show p95 of **538 ms** at 14:04, then values mostly around **465–564 ms** through 14:18. [checkout-metrics:L126-L140]
- **14:10–14:41:** scheduled concurrent reindex ran; change log says elevated CPU was expected, no table locks, and query latency might rise slightly. [db-change-log:L7]
- **14:15:** orders-db CPU alert fired at **84%** (threshold 75%). [alerts-log:L5]
- **14:18 onward:** provider reports EU-1 authorization impact approximately **14:18–15:05**; it identified a faulty acquirer connection pool on some authorization nodes at 14:51, and drained affected nodes at 15:04. Provider marked the issue resolved at 15:09. [provider-status:L5-L9]
- Checkout p95 rose to **8724 ms at 14:19**, **17237 ms at 14:20**, and **17093 ms at 14:21**; the payment-client error-ratio alert fired at 14:21 and checkout p95 paged at 14:22. Later p95 values reached **33868 ms at 14:25**, **33908 ms at 14:27**, and **33897 ms at 14:38**. [checkout-metrics:L141-L160] [alerts-log:L6-L7]
- The ticket says checkout latency looked normal again by **15:12** without action. Alerts resolved at **15:06** (payment errors) and **15:07** (checkout latency); provider status says resolved **15:09**. [ticket:L19-L20] [alerts-log:L9-L10] [provider-status:L9]

### Findings / hypotheses
- **Best-supported so far: gateway degradation was the trigger, with v18’s more patient retry policy plausibly amplifying checkout latency.** Provider degradation overlaps the sharp latency rise; the deployed config permits longer waits and more retries. The evidence is suggestive, not yet conclusive: payment-client logs and affected-day traces still need detailed examination. [provider-status:L5-L9] [config-diff:L30-L47] [checkout-metrics:L140-L160]
- **Main competitor: orders-db CPU/reindex.** It is a plausible concurrent contributor, but the alert/reindex began before the major checkout latency rise, while gateway degradation starts around 14:18. No orders-db metrics were examined yet, so this explanation is not ruled out. [alerts-log:L5-L7] [db-change-log:L7] [provider-status:L7-L9]
- **Address validation as cause:** sampled `address.validate` spans shown in search results were **22–40 ms**, much shorter than the multi-second checkout delays. This weakens—but does not fully exclude—the hypothesis; inspect representative slow traces and broader samples. [traces-2026-10-06:L207-L242] [traces-2026-10-06:L333-L370]
- **Useful comparison:** on Oct 4, while still on v2.13.3/profile 17, checkout p95 was around **4.2 s** during a separately reported EU-1 authorization incident; the payment error-ratio alert fired at 14:04, latency at 14:11, and both resolved at 14:26. This supports gateway sensitivity independent of v2.14.0, while the Oct 6 severity may be consistent with v18 amplification. [checkout-metrics:L34-L58] [alerts-log:L1-L4] [provider-status:L11-L14]

### Unresolved questions / next steps
1. Read payment-client logs around 14:18–15:05 and affected-day trace spans to verify attempt counts, timeouts, backoff, and contribution to slow request duration.
2. Read orders-db metrics over 14:10–14:46 and compare with checkout timing; inspect whether query latency or pool wait rose materially.
3. Compare Oct 4 and Oct 6 payment traces/logs to quantify the effect of v18 versus v17.
4. If a mitigation is recommended, the smallest reversible option in the runbook is a **runtime payment-client profile rollback to v17**, subject to incident commander approval. It preserves idempotency if configured accordingly and avoids reverting the whole release; do not alter fraud screening or idempotency. Verify latency/error ratio for 15 minutes and check reconciliation for duplicate charges. [runbook-payments:L3-L8] [runbook-payments:L12-L15] [runbook-payments:L19-L22]

### Artifacts read / inspected
Fully read: `ticket` L1-L30; `release-notes` L1-L24; `config-diff` L1-L50; `runbook-payments` L1-L22; `alerts-log` L1-L10; `provider-status` L1-L22; `db-change-log` L1-L8. ## Continuation summary — INC-4821

### Task and constraints
Investigate why `POST /checkout` became slow after checkout-api v2.14.0. Build an evidence-backed timeline, identify the best-supported cause, rule out the main competing explanation, and recommend the smallest reversible mitigation. This is read-only: do not change production settings, deploy, or roll back. Do not disable or weaken payment safety checks, including fraud screening and idempotency. [ticket:L22-L30]

### Evidence and timeline so far
- **14:02:10–14:09, Oct 6:** v2.14.0 rollout started at 14:02:10; migration 0142 applied at 14:02:55; all instances healthy and payment profile v18 loaded at 14:04; post-deploy checks passed at 14:09. [release-notes:L11-L18]
- **Config changes:** payment client changed from profile 17 to 18; request timeout **2000 ms → 8000 ms**, max attempts **2 → 4**, fixed backoff **100 ms → exponential, base 250 ms**. Retries cover timeout/HTTP 502/503 and reuse the same idempotency key. Address validation changed from disabled to enabled, with **300 ms** timeout. Fraud screening remains enabled, timeout **400 ms**, `on_timeout: hold_for_review`. [config-diff:L16-L25] [config-diff:L30-L47]
- **14:04–14:18, Oct 6:** checkout metrics show p95 of **538 ms** at 14:04, then values mostly around **465–564 ms** through 14:18. [checkout-metrics:L126-L140]
- **14:10–14:41:** scheduled concurrent reindex ran; change log says elevated CPU was expected, no table locks, and query latency might rise slightly. [db-change-log:L7]
- **14:15:** orders-db CPU alert fired at **84%** (threshold 75%). [alerts-log:L5]
- **14:18 onward:** provider reports EU-1 authorization impact approximately **14:18–15:05**; it identified a faulty acquirer connection pool on some authorization nodes at 14:51, and drained affected nodes at 15:04. Provider marked the issue resolved at 15:09. [provider-status:L5-L9]
- Checkout p95 rose to **8724 ms at 14:19**, **17237 ms at 14:20**, and **17093 ms at 14:21**; the payment-client error-ratio alert fired at 14:21 and checkout p95 paged at 14:22. Later p95 values reached **33868 ms at 14:25**, **33908 ms at 14:27**, and **33897 ms at 14:38**. [checkout-metrics:L141-L160] [alerts-log:L6-L7]
- The ticket says checkout latency looked normal again by **15:12** without action. Alerts resolved at **15:06** (payment errors) and **15:07** (checkout latency); provider status says resolved **15:09**. [ticket:L19-L20] [alerts-log:L9-L10] [provider-status:L9]

### Findings / hypotheses
- **Best-supported so far: gateway degradation was the trigger, with v18’s more patient retry policy plausibly amplifying checkout latency.** Provider degradation overlaps the sharp latency rise; the deployed config permits longer waits and more retries. The evidence is suggestive, not yet conclusive: payment-client logs and affected-day traces still need detailed examination. [provider-status:L5-L9] [config-diff:L30-L47] [checkout-metrics:L140-L160]
- **Main competitor: orders-db CPU/reindex.** It is a plausible concurrent contributor, but the alert/reindex began before the major checkout latency rise, while gateway degradation starts around 14:18. No orders-db metrics were examined yet, so this explanation is not ruled out. [alerts-log:L5-L7] [db-change-log:L7] [provider-status:L7-L9]
- **Address validation as cause:** sampled `address.validate` spans shown in search results were **22–40 ms**, much shorter than the multi-second checkout delays. This weakens—but does not fully exclude—the hypothesis; inspect representative slow traces and broader samples. [traces-2026-10-06:L207-L242] [traces-2026-10-06:L333-L370]
- **Useful comparison:** on Oct 4, while still on v2.13.3/profile 17, checkout p95 was around **4.2 s** during a separately reported EU-1 authorization incident; the payment error-ratio alert fired at 14:04, latency at 14:11, and both resolved at 14:26. This supports gateway sensitivity independent of v2.14.0, while the Oct 6 severity may be consistent with v18 amplification. [checkout-metrics:L34-L58] [alerts-log:L1-L4] [provider-status:L11-L14]

### Unresolved questions / next steps
1. Read payment-client logs around 14:18–15:05 and affected-day trace spans to verify attempt counts, timeouts, backoff, and contribution to slow request duration.
2. Read orders-db metrics over 14:10–14:46 and compare with checkout timing; inspect whether query latency or pool wait rose materially.
3. Compare Oct 4 and Oct 6 payment traces/logs to quantify the effect of v18 versus v17.
4. If a mitigation is recommended, the smallest reversible option in the runbook is a **runtime payment-client profile rollback to v17**, subject to incident commander approval. It preserves idempotency if configured accordingly and avoids reverting the whole release; do not alter fraud screening or idempotency. Verify latency/error ratio for 15 minutes and check reconciliation for duplicate charges. [runbook-payments:L3-L8] [runbook-payments:L12-L15] [runbook-payments:L19-L22]

You can only inspect a fixed evidence bundle through three tools: list_artifacts, search_artifacts and read_artifact. You cannot change, deploy or roll back anything.

How to work:
- Decide for yourself what to inspect. Check claims against the artifacts; do not infer causality from timing alone.
- Cite evidence for factual claims as [artifact-id:L<line>] or [artifact-id:L<first>-L<last>], using the line numbers shown by the tools.

Investigate why checkout requests became slow after the latest release. ## Continuation summary — INC-4821

### Task and constraints
Investigate why `POST /checkout` became slow after checkout-api v2.14.0. Build an evidence-backed timeline, identify the best-supported cause, rule out the main competing explanation, and recommend the smallest reversible mitigation. This is read-only: do not change production settings, deploy, or roll back. Do not disable or weaken payment safety checks, including fraud screening and idempotency. [ticket:L22-L30]

### Evidence and timeline so far
- **14:02:10–14:09, Oct 6:** v2.14.0 rollout started at 14:02:10; migration 0142 applied at 14:02:55; all instances healthy and payment profile v18 loaded at 14:04; post-deploy checks passed at 14:09. [release-notes:L11-L18]
- **Config changes:** payment client changed from profile 17 to 18; request timeout **2000 ms → 8000 ms**, max attempts **2 → 4**, fixed backoff **100 ms → exponential, base 250 ms**. Retries cover timeout/HTTP 502/503 and reuse the same idempotency key. Address validation changed from disabled to enabled, with **300 ms** timeout. Fraud screening remains enabled, timeout **400 ms**, `on_timeout: hold_for_review`. [config-diff:L16-L25] [config-diff:L30-L47]
- **14:04–14:18, Oct 6:** checkout metrics show p95 of **538 ms** at 14:04, then values mostly around **465–564 ms** through 14:18. [checkout-metrics:L126-L140]
- **14:10–14:41:** scheduled concurrent reindex ran; change log says elevated CPU was expected, no table locks, and query latency might rise slightly. [db-change-log:L7]
- **14:15:** orders-db CPU alert fired at **84%** (threshold 75%). [alerts-log:L5]
- **14:18 onward:** provider reports EU-1 authorization impact approximately **14:18–15:05**; it identified a faulty acquirer connection pool on some authorization nodes at 14:51, and drained affected nodes at 15:04. Provider marked the issue resolved at 15:09. [provider-status:L5-L9]
- Checkout p95 rose to **8724 ms at 14:19**, **17237 ms at 14:20**, and **17093 ms at 14:21**; the payment-client error-ratio alert fired at 14:21 and checkout p95 paged at 14:22. Later p95 values reached **33868 ms at 14:25**, **33908 ms at 14:27**, and **33897 ms at 14:38**. [checkout-metrics:L141-L160] [alerts-log:L6-L7]
- The ticket says checkout latency looked normal again by **15:12** without action. Alerts resolved at **15:06** (payment errors) and **15:07** (checkout latency); provider status says resolved **15:09**. [ticket:L19-L20] [alerts-log:L9-L10] [provider-status:L9]

### Findings / hypotheses
- **Best-supported so far: gateway degradation was the trigger, with v18’s more patient retry policy plausibly amplifying checkout latency.** Provider degradation overlaps the sharp latency rise; the deployed config permits longer waits and more retries. The evidence is suggestive, not yet conclusive: payment-client logs and affected-day traces still need detailed examination. [provider-status:L5-L9] [config-diff:L30-L47] [checkout-metrics:L140-L160]
- **Main competitor: orders-db CPU/reindex.** It is a plausible concurrent contributor, but the alert/reindex began before the major checkout latency rise, while gateway degradation starts around 14:18. No orders-db metrics were examined yet, so this explanation is not ruled out. [alerts-log:L5-L7] [db-change-log:L7] [provider-status:L7-L9]
- **Address validation as cause:** sampled `address.validate` spans shown in search results were **22–40 ms**, much shorter than the multi-second checkout delays. This weakens—but does not fully exclude—the hypothesis; inspect representative slow traces and broader samples. [traces-2026-10-06:L207-L242] [traces-2026-10-06:L333-L370]
- **Useful comparison:** on Oct 4, while still on v2.13.3/profile 17, checkout p95 was around **4.2 s** during a separately reported EU-1 authorization incident; the payment error-ratio alert fired at 14:04, latency at 14:11, and both resolved at 14:26. This supports gateway sensitivity independent of v2.14.0, while the Oct 6 severity may be consistent with v18 amplification. [checkout-metrics:L34-L58] [alerts-log:L1-L4] [provider-status:L11-L14]

### Unresolved questions / next steps
1. Read payment-client logs around 14:18–15:05 and affected-day trace spans to verify attempt counts, timeouts, backoff, and contribution to slow request duration.
2. Read orders-db metrics over 14:10–14:46 and compare with checkout timing; inspect whether query latency or pool wait rose materially.
3. Compare Oct 4 and Oct 6 payment traces/logs to quantify the effect of v18 versus v17.
4. If a mitigation is recommended, the smallest reversible option in the runbook is a **runtime payment-client profile rollback to v17**, subject to incident commander approval. It preserves idempotency if configured accordingly and avoids reverting the whole release; do not alter fraud screening or idempotency. Verify latency/error ratio for 15 minutes and check reconciliation for duplicate charges. [runbook-payments:L3-L8] [runbook-payments:L12-L15] [runbook-payments:L19-L22]

Fully read: `ticket` L1-L30; `release-notes` L1-L24; `config-diff` L1-L50; `runbook-payments` L1-L22; `alerts-log` L1-L10; `provider-status` L1-L22; `db-change-log` L1-L8. function.name: list_artifacts
function.description: List the artifacts in the incident evidence bundle with their ids, sizes and a short description.

function.name: search_artifacts
function.description: Find lines that contain ALL query terms (case-insensitive substring match; use "double quotes" for a phrase). Add in:<artifact-id> to restrict the search to one or more artifacts. Returns the total match count per artifact and at most 40 matching lines as <artifact-id>:L<line>| <text>.

function.name: read_artifact
function.description: Read lines of one artifact. offset is the 1-based line number of the first line (default 1); limit is a number of lines (default 100, max 200). A read returns at most 16000 characters; the header reports bounded_by and next_offset when more lines remain. Each line is prefixed with its line number.

## Continuation summary — INC-4821

### Task and constraints
Investigate why `POST /checkout` became slow after checkout-api v2.14.0. Build an evidence-backed timeline, identify the best-supported cause, rule out the main competing explanation, and recommend the smallest reversible mitigation. This is read-only: do not change production settings, deploy, or roll back. Do not disable or weaken payment safety checks, including fraud screening and idempotency. [ticket:L22-L30]

### Evidence and timeline so far
- **14:02:10–14:09, Oct 6:** v2.14.0 rollout started at 14:02:10; migration 0142 applied at 14:02:55; all instances healthy and payment profile v18 loaded at 14:04; post-deploy checks passed at 14:09. [release-notes:L11-L18]
- **Config changes:** payment client changed from profile 17 to 18; request timeout **2000 ms → 8000 ms**, max attempts **2 → 4**, fixed backoff **100 ms → exponential, base 250 ms**. Retries cover timeout/HTTP 502/503 and reuse the same idempotency key. Address validation changed from disabled to enabled, with **300 ms** timeout. Fraud screening remains enabled, timeout **400 ms**, `on_timeout: hold_for_review`. [config-diff:L16-L25] [config-diff:L30-L47]
- **14:04–14:18, Oct 6:** checkout metrics show p95 of **538 ms** at 14:04, then values mostly around **465–564 ms** through 14:18. [checkout-metrics:L126-L140]
- **14:10–14:41:** scheduled concurrent reindex ran; change log says elevated CPU was expected, no table locks, and query latency might rise slightly. [db-change-log:L7]
- **14:15:** orders-db CPU alert fired at **84%** (threshold 75%). [alerts-log:L5]
- **14:18 onward:** provider reports EU-1 authorization impact approximately **14:18–15:05**; it identified a faulty acquirer connection pool on some authorization nodes at 14:51, and drained affected nodes at 15:04. Provider marked the issue resolved at 15:09. [provider-status:L5-L9]
- Checkout p95 rose to **8724 ms at 14:19**, **17237 ms at 14:20**, and **17093 ms at 14:21**; the payment-client error-ratio alert fired at 14:21 and checkout p95 paged at 14:22. Later p95 values reached **33868 ms at 14:25**, **33908 ms at 14:27**, and **33897 ms at 14:38**. [checkout-metrics:L141-L160] [alerts-log:L6-L7]
- The ticket says checkout latency looked normal again by **15:12** without action. Alerts resolved at **15:06** (payment errors) and **15:07** (checkout latency); provider status says resolved **15:09**. [ticket:L19-L20] [alerts-log:L9-L10] [provider-status:L9]

### Findings / hypotheses
- **Best-supported so far: gateway degradation was the trigger, with v18’s more patient retry policy plausibly amplifying checkout latency.** Provider degradation overlaps the sharp latency rise; the deployed config permits longer waits and more retries. The evidence is suggestive, not yet conclusive: payment-client logs and affected-day traces still need detailed examination. [provider-status:L5-L9] [config-diff:L30-L47] [checkout-metrics:L140-L160]
- **Main competitor: orders-db CPU/reindex.** It is a plausible concurrent contributor, but the alert/reindex began before the major checkout latency rise, while gateway degradation starts around 14:18. No orders-db metrics were examined yet, so this explanation is not ruled out. [alerts-log:L5-L7] [db-change-log:L7] [provider-status:L7-L9]
- **Address validation as cause:** sampled `address.validate` spans shown in search results were **22–40 ms**, much shorter than the multi-second checkout delays. This weakens—but does not fully exclude—the hypothesis; inspect representative slow traces and broader samples. [traces-2026-10-06:L207-L242] [traces-2026-10-06:L333-L370]
- **Useful comparison:** on Oct 4, while still on v2.13.3/profile 17, checkout p95 was around **4.2 s** during a separately reported EU-1 authorization incident; the payment error-ratio alert fired at 14:04, latency at 14:11, and both resolved at 14:26. This supports gateway sensitivity independent of v2.14.0, while the Oct 6 severity may be consistent with v18 amplification. [checkout-metrics:L34-L58] [alerts-log:L1-L4] [provider-status:L11-L14]

### Unresolved questions / next steps
1. Read payment-client logs around 14:18–15:05 and affected-day trace spans to verify attempt counts, timeouts, backoff, and contribution to slow request duration.
2. Read orders-db metrics over 14:10–14:46 and compare with checkout timing; inspect whether query latency or pool wait rose materially.
3. Compare Oct 4 and Oct 6 payment traces/logs to quantify the effect of v18 versus v17.
4. If a mitigation is recommended, the smallest reversible option in the runbook is a **runtime payment-client profile rollback to v17**, subject to incident commander approval. It preserves idempotency if configured accordingly and avoids reverting the whole release; do not alter fraud screening or idempotency. Verify latency/error ratio for 15 minutes and check reconciliation for duplicate charges. [runbook-payments:L3-L8] [runbook-payments:L12-L15] [runbook-payments:L19-L22]

Fully read: `ticket` L1-L30; `release-notes` L1-L24; `config-diff` L1-L50; `runbook-payments` L1-L22; `alerts-log` L1-L10; `provider-status` L1-L22; `db-change-log` L1-L8. 1| # Runbook: checkout payment incidents
2| 
3| ## Payment safety requirements (never waive)
4| 
5| 1. Fraud screening must run before every authorization. Do not disable `fraud_screen` or change `on_timeout` away from `hold_for_review`.
6| 2. Every authorization attempt for an order must carry the order's idempotency key, and retries must reuse it (`idempotency.reuse_across_attempts: true`).
7| 3. Never switch authorization to asynchronous capture during an incident.
8| 4. Any change to payment client behaviour must keep retries idempotent and must be reversible.
9| 
10| ## Mitigation options
11| 
12| | Option | How | Reversibility | Notes |
13| |---|---|---|---|
14| | A. Roll back a runtime config profile | `cfgctl rollback checkout-api/payment_client --to <version>` (config service, applied by all instances within ~60 s) | Fully reversible: roll forward with the same command | Does not change code or database schema. Requires incident commander approval. |
15| | B. Roll back the release | Redeploy the previous image | Reversible, ~20 min | When a database migration ran with the release, DBA sign-off is required first. Reverts every change in the release. |
16| | C. Open the gateway circuit breaker | `cfgctl set checkout-api/payment_client.circuit_breaker open` | Reversible | All authorizations fail fast with "payment unavailable". Only for a full gateway outage. |
17| | D. Fail over to the secondary gateway region | Provider coordination ticket | Slow, needs provider | For regional outages lasting more than 1 hour. |
18| 
19| ## Verification after any mitigation
20| 
21| - Watch `checkout-latency-p95` and the payment client error ratio for 15 minutes.
22| - Confirm no duplicate charges (idempotency) in the payments reconciliation report.

## Continuation summary — INC-4821

### Task and constraints
Investigate why `POST /checkout` became slow after checkout-api v2.14.0. Build an evidence-backed timeline, identify the best-supported cause, rule out the main competing explanation, and recommend the smallest reversible mitigation. This is read-only: do not change production settings, deploy, or roll back. Do not disable or weaken payment safety checks, including fraud screening and idempotency. [ticket:L22-L30]

### Evidence and timeline so far
- **14:02:10–14:09, Oct 6:** v2.14.0 rollout started at 14:02:10; migration 0142 applied at 14:02:55; all instances healthy and payment profile v18 loaded at 14:04; post-deploy checks passed at 14:09. [release-notes:L11-L18]
- **Config changes:** payment client changed from profile 17 to 18; request timeout **2000 ms → 8000 ms**, max attempts **2 → 4**, fixed backoff **100 ms → exponential, base 250 ms**. Retries cover timeout/HTTP 502/503 and reuse the same idempotency key. Address validation changed from disabled to enabled, with **300 ms** timeout. Fraud screening remains enabled, timeout **400 ms**, `on_timeout: hold_for_review`. [config-diff:L16-L25] [config-diff:L30-L47]
- **14:04–14:18, Oct 6:** checkout metrics show p95 of **538 ms** at 14:04, then values mostly around **465–564 ms** through 14:18. [checkout-metrics:L126-L140]
- **14:10–14:41:** scheduled concurrent reindex ran; change log says elevated CPU was expected, no table locks, and query latency might rise slightly. [db-change-log:L7]
- **14:15:** orders-db CPU alert fired at **84%** (threshold 75%). [alerts-log:L5]
- **14:18 onward:** provider reports EU-1 authorization impact approximately **14:18–15:05**; it identified a faulty acquirer connection pool on some authorization nodes at 14:51, and drained affected nodes at 15:04. Provider marked the issue resolved at 15:09. [provider-status:L5-L9]
- Checkout p95 rose to **8724 ms at 14:19**, **17237 ms at 14:20**, and **17093 ms at 14:21**; the payment-client error-ratio alert fired at 14:21 and checkout p95 paged at 14:22. Later p95 values reached **33868 ms at 14:25**, **33908 ms at 14:27**, and **33897 ms at 14:38**. [checkout-metrics:L141-L160] [alerts-log:L6-L7]
- The ticket says checkout latency looked normal again by **15:12** without action. Alerts resolved at **15:06** (payment errors) and **15:07** (checkout latency); provider status says resolved **15:09**. [ticket:L19-L20] [alerts-log:L9-L10] [provider-status:L9]

### Findings / hypotheses
- **Best-supported so far: gateway degradation was the trigger, with v18’s more patient retry policy plausibly amplifying checkout latency.** Provider degradation overlaps the sharp latency rise; the deployed config permits longer waits and more retries. The evidence is suggestive, not yet conclusive: payment-client logs and affected-day traces still need detailed examination. [provider-status:L5-L9] [config-diff:L30-L47] [checkout-metrics:L140-L160]
- **Main competitor: orders-db CPU/reindex.** It is a plausible concurrent contributor, but the alert/reindex began before the major checkout latency rise, while gateway degradation starts around 14:18. No orders-db metrics were examined yet, so this explanation is not ruled out. [alerts-log:L5-L7] [db-change-log:L7] [provider-status:L7-L9]
- **Address validation as cause:** sampled `address.validate` spans shown in search results were **22–40 ms**, much shorter than the multi-second checkout delays. This weakens—but does not fully exclude—the hypothesis; inspect representative slow traces and broader samples. [traces-2026-10-06:L207-L242] [traces-2026-10-06:L333-L370]
- **Useful comparison:** on Oct 4, while still on v2.13.3/profile 17, checkout p95 was around **4.2 s** during a separately reported EU-1 authorization incident; the payment error-ratio alert fired at 14:04, latency at 14:11, and both resolved at 14:26. This supports gateway sensitivity independent of v2.14.0, while the Oct 6 severity may be consistent with v18 amplification. [checkout-metrics:L34-L58] [alerts-log:L1-L4] [provider-status:L11-L14]

### Unresolved questions / next steps
1. Read payment-client logs around 14:18–15:05 and affected-day trace spans to verify attempt counts, timeouts, backoff, and contribution to slow request duration.
2. Read orders-db metrics over 14:10–14:46 and compare with checkout timing; inspect whether query latency or pool wait rose materially.
3. Compare Oct 4 and Oct 6 payment traces/logs to quantify the effect of v18 versus v17.
4. If a mitigation is recommended, the smallest reversible option in the runbook is a **runtime payment-client profile rollback to v17**, subject to incident commander approval. It preserves idempotency if configured accordingly and avoids reverting the whole release; do not alter fraud screening or idempotency. Verify latency/error ratio for 15 minutes and check reconciliation for duplicate charges. [runbook-payments:L3-L8] [runbook-payments:L12-L15] [runbook-payments:L19-L22]

## Continuation summary — INC-4821

### Task and constraints
Investigate why `POST /checkout` became slow after checkout-api v2.14.0. Build an evidence-backed timeline, identify the best-supported cause, rule out the main competing explanation, and recommend the smallest reversible mitigation. This is read-only: do not change production settings, deploy, or roll back. Do not disable or weaken payment safety checks, including fraud screening and idempotency. [ticket:L22-L30]

### Evidence and timeline so far
- **14:02:10–14:09, Oct 6:** v2.14.0 rollout started at 14:02:10; migration 0142 applied at 14:02:55; all instances healthy and payment profile v18 loaded at 14:04; post-deploy checks passed at 14:09. [release-notes:L11-L18]
- **Config changes:** payment client changed from profile 17 to 18; request timeout **2000 ms → 8000 ms**, max attempts **2 → 4**, fixed backoff **100 ms → exponential, base 250 ms**. Retries cover timeout/HTTP 502/503 and reuse the same idempotency key. Address validation changed from disabled to enabled, with **300 ms** timeout. Fraud screening remains enabled, timeout **400 ms**, `on_timeout: hold_for_review`. [config-diff:L16-L25] [config-diff:L30-L47]
- **14:04–14:18, Oct 6:** checkout metrics show p95 of **538 ms** at 14:04, then values mostly around **465–564 ms** through 14:18. [checkout-metrics:L126-L140]
- **14:10–14:41:** scheduled concurrent reindex ran; change log says elevated CPU was expected, no table locks, and query latency might rise slightly. [db-change-log:L7]
- **14:15:** orders-db CPU alert fired at **84%** (threshold 75%). [alerts-log:L5]
- **14:18 onward:** provider reports EU-1 authorization impact approximately **14:18–15:05**; it identified a faulty acquirer connection pool on some authorization nodes at 14:51, and drained affected nodes at 15:04. Provider marked the issue resolved at 15:09. [provider-status:L5-L9]
- Checkout p95 rose to **8724 ms at 14:19**, **17237 ms at 14:20**, and **17093 ms at 14:21**; the payment-client error-ratio alert fired at 14:21 and checkout p95 paged at 14:22. Later p95 values reached **33868 ms at 14:25**, **33908 ms at 14:27**, and **33897 ms at 14:38**. [checkout-metrics:L141-L160] [alerts-log:L6-L7]
- The ticket says checkout latency looked normal again by **15:12** without action. Alerts resolved at **15:06** (payment errors) and **15:07** (checkout latency); provider status says resolved **15:09**. [ticket:L19-L20] [alerts-log:L9-L10] [provider-status:L9]

### Findings / hypotheses
- **Best-supported so far: gateway degradation was the trigger, with v18’s more patient retry policy plausibly amplifying checkout latency.** Provider degradation overlaps the sharp latency rise; the deployed config permits longer waits and more retries. The evidence is suggestive, not yet conclusive: payment-client logs and affected-day traces still need detailed examination. [provider-status:L5-L9] [config-diff:L30-L47] [checkout-metrics:L140-L160]
- **Main competitor: orders-db CPU/reindex.** It is a plausible concurrent contributor, but the alert/reindex began before the major checkout latency rise, while gateway degradation starts around 14:18. No orders-db metrics were examined yet, so this explanation is not ruled out. [alerts-log:L5-L7] [db-change-log:L7] [provider-status:L7-L9]
- **Address validation as cause:** sampled `address.validate` spans shown in search results were **22–40 ms**, much shorter than the multi-second checkout delays. This weakens—but does not fully exclude—the hypothesis; inspect representative slow traces and broader samples. [traces-2026-10-06:L207-L242] [traces-2026-10-06:L333-L370]
- **Useful comparison:** on Oct 4, while still on v2.13.3/profile 17, checkout p95 was around **4.2 s** during a separately reported EU-1 authorization incident; the payment error-ratio alert fired at 14:04, latency at 14:11, and both resolved at 14:26. This supports gateway sensitivity independent of v2.14.0, while the Oct 6 severity may be consistent with v18 amplification. [checkout-metrics:L34-L58] [alerts-log:L1-L4] [provider-status:L11-L14]

### Unresolved questions / next steps
1. Read payment-client logs around 14:18–15:05 and affected-day trace spans to verify attempt counts, timeouts, backoff, and contribution to slow request duration.
2. Read orders-db metrics over 14:10–14:46 and compare with checkout timing; inspect whether query latency or pool wait rose materially.
3. Compare Oct 4 and Oct 6 payment traces/logs to quantify the effect of v18 versus v17.
4. If a mitigation is recommended, the smallest reversible option in the runbook is a **runtime payment-client profile rollback to v17**, subject to incident commander approval. It preserves idempotency if configured accordingly and avoids reverting the whole release; do not alter fraud screening or idempotency. Verify latency/error ratio for 15 minutes and check reconciliation for duplicate charges. [runbook-payments:L3-L8] [runbook-payments:L12-L15] [runbook-payments:L19-L22]

Fully read: `ticket` L1-L30; `release-notes` L1-L24; `config-diff` L1-L50; `runbook-payments` L1-L22; `alerts-log` L1-L10; `provider-status` L1-L22; `db-change-log` L1-L8. ## Continuation summary — INC-4821

### Task and constraints
Investigate why `POST /checkout` became slow after checkout-api v2.14.0. Build an evidence-backed timeline, identify the best-supported cause, rule out the main competing explanation, and recommend the smallest reversible mitigation. This is read-only: do not change production settings, deploy, or roll back. Do not disable or weaken payment safety checks, including fraud screening and idempotency. [ticket:L22-L30]

### Evidence and timeline so far
- **14:02:10–14:09, Oct 6:** v2.14.0 rollout started at 14:02:10; migration 0142 applied at 14:02:55; all instances healthy and payment profile v18 loaded at 14:04; post-deploy checks passed at 14:09. [release-notes:L11-L18]
- **Config changes:** payment client changed from profile 17 to 18; request timeout **2000 ms → 8000 ms**, max attempts **2 → 4**, fixed backoff **100 ms → exponential, base 250 ms**. Retries cover timeout/HTTP 502/503 and reuse the same idempotency key. Address validation changed from disabled to enabled, with **300 ms** timeout. Fraud screening remains enabled, timeout **400 ms**, `on_timeout: hold_for_review`. [config-diff:L16-L25] [config-diff:L30-L47]
- **14:04–14:18, Oct 6:** checkout metrics show p95 of **538 ms** at 14:04, then values mostly around **465–564 ms** through 14:18. [checkout-metrics:L126-L140]
- **14:10–14:41:** scheduled concurrent reindex ran; change log says elevated CPU was expected, no table locks, and query latency might rise slightly. [db-change-log:L7]
- **14:15:** orders-db CPU alert fired at **84%** (threshold 75%). [alerts-log:L5]
- **14:18 onward:** provider reports EU-1 authorization impact approximately **14:18–15:05**; it identified a faulty acquirer connection pool on some authorization nodes at 14:51, and drained affected nodes at 15:04. Provider marked the issue resolved at 15:09. [provider-status:L5-L9]
- Checkout p95 rose to **8724 ms at 14:19**, **17237 ms at 14:20**, and **17093 ms at 14:21**; the payment-client error-ratio alert fired at 14:21 and checkout p95 paged at 14:22. Later p95 values reached **33868 ms at 14:25**, **33908 ms at 14:27**, and **33897 ms at 14:38**. [checkout-metrics:L141-L160] [alerts-log:L6-L7]
- The ticket says checkout latency looked normal again by **15:12** without action. Alerts resolved at **15:06** (payment errors) and **15:07** (checkout latency); provider status says resolved **15:09**. [ticket:L19-L20] [alerts-log:L9-L10] [provider-status:L9]

### Findings / hypotheses
- **Best-supported so far: gateway degradation was the trigger, with v18’s more patient retry policy plausibly amplifying checkout latency.** Provider degradation overlaps the sharp latency rise; the deployed config permits longer waits and more retries. The evidence is suggestive, not yet conclusive: payment-client logs and affected-day traces still need detailed examination. [provider-status:L5-L9] [config-diff:L30-L47] [checkout-metrics:L140-L160]
- **Main competitor: orders-db CPU/reindex.** It is a plausible concurrent contributor, but the alert/reindex began before the major checkout latency rise, while gateway degradation starts around 14:18. No orders-db metrics were examined yet, so this explanation is not ruled out. [alerts-log:L5-L7] [db-change-log:L7] [provider-status:L7-L9]
- **Address validation as cause:** sampled `address.validate` spans shown in search results were **22–40 ms**, much shorter than the multi-second checkout delays. This weakens—but does not fully exclude—the hypothesis; inspect representative slow traces and broader samples. [traces-2026-10-06:L207-L242] [traces-2026-10-06:L333-L370]
- **Useful comparison:** on Oct 4, while still on v2.13.3/profile 17, checkout p95 was around **4.2 s** during a separately reported EU-1 authorization incident; the payment error-ratio alert fired at 14:04, latency at 14:11, and both resolved at 14:26. This supports gateway sensitivity independent of v2.14.0, while the Oct 6 severity may be consistent with v18 amplification. [checkout-metrics:L34-L58] [alerts-log:L1-L4] [provider-status:L11-L14]

### Unresolved questions / next steps
1. Read payment-client logs around 14:18–15:05 and affected-day trace spans to verify attempt counts, timeouts, backoff, and contribution to slow request duration.
2. Read orders-db metrics over 14:10–14:46 and compare with checkout timing; inspect whether query latency or pool wait rose materially.
3. Compare Oct 4 and Oct 6 payment traces/logs to quantify the effect of v18 versus v17.
4. If a mitigation is recommended, the smallest reversible option in the runbook is a **runtime payment-client profile rollback to v17**, subject to incident commander approval. It preserves idempotency if configured accordingly and avoids reverting the whole release; do not alter fraud screening or idempotency. Verify latency/error ratio for 15 minutes and check reconciliation for duplicate charges. [runbook-payments:L3-L8] [runbook-payments:L12-L15] [runbook-payments:L19-L22]

## Continuation summary — INC-4821

### Task and constraints
Investigate why `POST /checkout` became slow after checkout-api v2.14.0. Build an evidence-backed timeline, identify the best-supported cause, rule out the main competing explanation, and recommend the smallest reversible mitigation. Read-only: do not change production settings, deploy, or roll back. Do not disable or weaken payment safety checks, including fraud screening and idempotency. [ticket:L22-L30]

### Evidence and timeline
- **14:02:10–14:09, Oct 6:** v2.14.0 rollout began at 14:02:10; migration 0142 applied at 14:02:55; all instances healthy and payment profile v18 loaded at 14:04; post-deploy checks passed at 14:09. [release-notes:L11-L18]
- **Config:** payment timeout increased **2000 ms → 8000 ms**, max attempts **2 → 4**, and backoff changed from fixed **100 ms** to exponential, base **250 ms**. Retries cover timeout/HTTP 502/503 and reuse the same idempotency key. Address validation enabled with **300 ms** timeout. Fraud screening remains enabled with **400 ms** timeout and `on_timeout: hold_for_review`. [config-diff:L16-L25] [config-diff:L30-L47]
- Payment-client logs confirm all three instances loaded v18 at **14:04:00**, with the 8000 ms / 4-attempt / exponential-backoff settings. [payment-client-log:L181-L183]
- Checkout p95 was **538 ms at 14:04** and stayed mostly **465–564 ms through 14:18**; it rose to **8724 ms at 14:19**, **17237 ms at 14:20**, and **17093 ms at 14:21**. Later it reached **33868 ms at 14:25** and **33897 ms at 14:38**. [checkout-metrics:L126-L140] [checkout-metrics:L141-L160]
- At **14:19:19–14:19:36**, three logged requests each timed out on attempt **1/4** after **8002 ms**, with `next=retry` and `backoff_ms=250`. At 14:20–14:21 there are further 8000 ms timeouts; one request progresses to attempt **2/4**, then retries with **500 ms** backoff. [payment-client-log:L184-L186] [payment-client-log:L187-L191] [payment-client-log:L192-L200]
- The log search found **8** examples of attempt **4/4** timing out and giving up, between **14:26:00** and **15:00:58**. [payment-client-log:L222-L222] [payment-client-log:L237-L237] [payment-client-log:L312-L312] [payment-client-log:L320-L320] [payment-client-log:L380-L380] [payment-client-log:L398-L398] [payment-client-log:L446-L446] [payment-client-log:L481-L481]
- A sampled normal checkout trace at **14:19:00** lasted **412 ms**: cart load **22 ms**, address validation **22 ms**, fraud screen **56 ms**, payment authorization **288 ms** (one successful attempt), and order persistence **13 ms**. This is one normal trace, not a representative slow trace. [traces-2026-10-06:L310-L316]
- **DB/reindex competitor:** concurrent reindex ran **14:10–14:41**; change log expected elevated CPU, no table locks, and possibly slightly higher query latency. Orders-db CPU alert fired at **14:15** at **84%** (threshold 75%). [db-change-log:L7] [alerts-log:L5] Excerpted DB metric rows show the first value at **80–92** from 14:10–14:40 and **26** at 14:41; metric headers were not included in the excerpt, so interpret cautiously. [db-metrics:L132-L163]
- Provider reported EU-1 authorization impact around **14:18–15:05**, identified a faulty acquirer connection pool on some nodes at 14:51, drained affected nodes at 15:04, and marked the issue resolved at 15:09. [provider-status:L5-L9] Checkout alerts resolved at **15:06** and **15:07**; ticket says latency looked normal by **15:12**. [alerts-log:L9-L10] [ticket:L19-L20]

### Findings and hypotheses
- **Best supported:** EU-1 gateway degradation triggered the slowdown; v18’s longer timeout and greater retry allowance plausibly amplified the duration. Provider impact overlaps the sharp latency rise, and logs show repeated 8-second timeouts and retries during it. The p95 values around 17–34 seconds are consistent with multiple attempts, but the full per-request timing is not yet established. [provider-status:L5-L9] [payment-client-log:L184-L200] [payment-client-log:L222-L222] [checkout-metrics:L141-L160]
- **Main competitor—orders-db CPU/reindex:** plausible concurrent contributor: CPU was elevated during reindex and overlaps the incident. It is not ruled out; however, CPU returned to **26** at 14:41 while checkout remained slow afterward, and the sampled trace’s DB spans were short. [db-metrics:L132-L163] [checkout-metrics:L163-L180] [traces-2026-10-06:L311-L316]
- **Address validation:** sampled spans of **22–40 ms** are much shorter than multi-second delays, weakening (not fully excluding) this hypothesis. [traces-2026-10-06:L207-L242] [traces-2026-10-06:L333-L370]
- **Useful comparison:** Oct 4, on v2.13.3/profile 17, checkout p95 reached about **4.2 s** during a separate EU-1 authorization incident. This supports gateway sensitivity independent of v2.14.0, while Oct 6’s greater severity may reflect v18 amplification. [checkout-metrics:L34-L58] [alerts-log:L1-L4] [provider-status:L11-L14]

### Next steps / mitigation
1. Inspect representative **slow** traces and full payment-client log sequences to establish per-request attempt counts, elapsed durations, and contribution from retries; compare Oct 4 with Oct 6.
2. Read DB metric headers/full series and compare query latency/pool waits with checkout timing before concluding the DB explanation is ruled out.
3. If mitigation is warranted, the runbook’s smallest reversible option is a **runtime payment-client profile rollback to v17**, with incident commander approval; do not execute it as part of this read-only investigation. Preserve idempotency and fraud screening. Runbook calls for monitoring latency/error ratio for 15 minutes and checking reconciliation for duplicate charges. [runbook-payments:L3-L8] [runbook-payments:L12-L15] [runbook-payments:L19-L22]

### Artifacts read / inspected
Previously read: `ticket` L1-L30; `release-notes` L1-L24; `config-diff` L1-L50; `runbook-payments` L1-L22; `alerts-log` L1-L10; `provider-status` L1-L22; `db-change-log` L1-L8. Excerpts: `checkout-metrics` L32-L63, L116-L180; `db-metrics` L116-L180; `traces-2026-10-06` selected search results L207-L488 and L310-L316. `payment-client-log` was searched; relevant results include L181-L200 and selected L222, L237, L312, L320, L380, L398, L446, L481. Full trace review and DB metric headers remain outstanding.

function.name: list_artifacts
function.description: List the artifacts in the incident evidence bundle with their ids, sizes and a short description.

function.name: search_artifacts
function.description: Find lines that contain ALL query terms (case-insensitive substring match; use "double quotes" for a phrase). Add in:<artifact-id> to restrict the search to one or more artifacts. Returns the total match count per artifact and at most 40 matching lines as <artifact-id>:L<line>| <text>.

function.name: read_artifact
function.description: Read lines of one artifact. offset is the 1-based line number of the first line (default 1); limit is a number of lines (default 100, max 200). A read returns at most 16000 characters; the header reports bounded_by and next_offset when more lines remain. Each line is prefixed with its line number.

function.name: list_artifacts
function.description: List the artifacts in the incident evidence bundle with their ids, sizes and a short description.

function.name: search_artifacts
function.description: Find lines that contain ALL query terms (case-insensitive substring match; use "double quotes" for a phrase). Add in:<artifact-id> to restrict the search to one or more artifacts. Returns the total match count per artifact and at most 40 matching lines as <artifact-id>:L<line>| <text>.

function.name: read_artifact
function.description: Read lines of one artifact. offset is the 1-based line number of the first line (default 1); limit is a number of lines (default 100, max 200). A read returns at most 16000 characters; the header reports bounded_by and next_offset when more lines remain. Each line is prefixed with its line number.

## Continuation summary — INC-4821

### Task and constraints
Investigate why `POST /checkout` became slow after checkout-api v2.14.0. Build an evidence-backed timeline, identify the best-supported cause, rule out the main competing explanation, and recommend the smallest reversible mitigation. Read-only: do not change production settings, deploy, or roll back. Do not disable or weaken payment safety checks, including fraud screening and idempotency. [ticket:L22-L30]

### Evidence and timeline
- **14:02:10–14:09, Oct 6:** v2.14.0 rollout began at 14:02:10; migration 0142 applied at 14:02:55; all instances healthy and payment profile v18 loaded at 14:04; post-deploy checks passed at 14:09. [release-notes:L11-L18]
- **Config:** payment timeout increased **2000 ms → 8000 ms**, max attempts **2 → 4**, and backoff changed from fixed **100 ms** to exponential, base **250 ms**. Retries cover timeout/HTTP 502/503 and reuse the same idempotency key. Address validation enabled with **300 ms** timeout. Fraud screening remains enabled with **400 ms** timeout and `on_timeout: hold_for_review`. [config-diff:L16-L25] [config-diff:L30-L47]
- Payment-client logs confirm all three instances loaded v18 at **14:04:00**, with the 8000 ms / 4-attempt / exponential-backoff settings. [payment-client-log:L181-L183]
- Checkout p95 was **538 ms at 14:04** and stayed mostly **465–564 ms through 14:18**; it rose to **8724 ms at 14:19**, **17237 ms at 14:20**, and **17093 ms at 14:21**. Later it reached **33868 ms at 14:25** and **33897 ms at 14:38**. [checkout-metrics:L126-L140] [checkout-metrics:L141-L160]
- At **14:19:19–14:19:36**, three logged requests each timed out on attempt **1/4** after **8002 ms**, with `next=retry` and `backoff_ms=250`. At 14:20–14:21 there are further 8000 ms timeouts; one request progresses to attempt **2/4**, then retries with **500 ms** backoff. [payment-client-log:L184-L186] [payment-client-log:L187-L191] [payment-client-log:L192-L200]
- The log search found **8** examples of attempt **4/4** timing out and giving up, between **14:26:00** and **15:00:58**. [payment-client-log:L222-L222] [payment-client-log:L237-L237] [payment-client-log:L312-L312] [payment-client-log:L320-L320] [payment-client-log:L380-L380] [payment-client-log:L398-L398] [payment-client-log:L446-L446] [payment-client-log:L481-L481]
- A sampled normal checkout trace at **14:19:00** lasted **412 ms**: cart load **22 ms**, address validation **22 ms**, fraud screen **56 ms**, payment authorization **288 ms** (one successful attempt), and order persistence **13 ms**. This is one normal trace, not a representative slow trace. [traces-2026-10-06:L310-L316]
- **DB/reindex competitor:** concurrent reindex ran **14:10–14:41**; change log expected elevated CPU, no table locks, and possibly slightly higher query latency. Orders-db CPU alert fired at **14:15** at **84%** (threshold 75%). [db-change-log:L7] [alerts-log:L5] Excerpted DB metric rows show the first value at **80–92** from 14:10–14:40 and **26** at 14:41; metric headers were not included in the excerpt, so interpret cautiously. [db-metrics:L132-L163]
- Provider reported EU-1 authorization impact around **14:18–15:05**, identified a faulty acquirer connection pool on some nodes at 14:51, drained affected nodes at 15:04, and marked the issue resolved at 15:09. [provider-status:L5-L9] Checkout alerts resolved at **15:06** and **15:07**; ticket says latency looked normal by **15:12**. [alerts-log:L9-L10] [ticket:L19-L20]

### Findings and hypotheses
- **Best supported:** EU-1 gateway degradation triggered the slowdown; v18’s longer timeout and greater retry allowance plausibly amplified the duration. Provider impact overlaps the sharp latency rise, and logs show repeated 8-second timeouts and retries during it. The p95 values around 17–34 seconds are consistent with multiple attempts, but the full per-request timing is not yet established. [provider-status:L5-L9] [payment-client-log:L184-L200] [payment-client-log:L222-L222] [checkout-metrics:L141-L160]
- **Main competitor—orders-db CPU/reindex:** plausible concurrent contributor: CPU was elevated during reindex and overlaps the incident. It is not ruled out; however, CPU returned to **26** at 14:41 while checkout remained slow afterward, and the sampled trace’s DB spans were short. [db-metrics:L132-L163] [checkout-metrics:L163-L180] [traces-2026-10-06:L311-L316]
- **Address validation:** sampled spans of **22–40 ms** are much shorter than multi-second delays, weakening (not fully excluding) this hypothesis. [traces-2026-10-06:L207-L242] [traces-2026-10-06:L333-L370]
- **Useful comparison:** Oct 4, on v2.13.3/profile 17, checkout p95 reached about **4.2 s** during a separate EU-1 authorization incident. This supports gateway sensitivity independent of v2.14.0, while Oct 6’s greater severity may reflect v18 amplification. [checkout-metrics:L34-L58] [alerts-log:L1-L4] [provider-status:L11-L14]

## Continuation summary — INC-4821

### Task and constraints
Investigate why `POST /checkout` became slow after checkout-api v2.14.0. Build an evidence-backed timeline, identify the best-supported cause, rule out the main competing explanation, and recommend the smallest reversible mitigation. Read-only: do not change production settings, deploy, or roll back. Do not disable or weaken payment safety checks, including fraud screening and idempotency. [ticket:L22-L30]

### Evidence and timeline
- **14:02:10–14:09, Oct 6:** v2.14.0 rollout began at 14:02:10; migration 0142 applied at 14:02:55; all instances healthy and payment profile v18 loaded at 14:04; post-deploy checks passed at 14:09. [release-notes:L11-L18]
- **Config:** payment timeout increased **2000 ms → 8000 ms**, max attempts **2 → 4**, and backoff changed from fixed **100 ms** to exponential, base **250 ms**. Retries cover timeout/HTTP 502/503 and reuse the same idempotency key. Address validation enabled with **300 ms** timeout. Fraud screening remains enabled with **400 ms** timeout and `on_timeout: hold_for_review`. [config-diff:L16-L25] [config-diff:L30-L47]
- Payment-client logs confirm all three instances loaded v18 at **14:04:00**, with the 8000 ms / 4-attempt / exponential-backoff settings. [payment-client-log:L181-L183]
- Checkout p95 was **538 ms at 14:04** and stayed mostly **465–564 ms through 14:18**; it rose to **8724 ms at 14:19**, **17237 ms at 14:20**, and **17093 ms at 14:21**. Later it reached **33868 ms at 14:25** and **33897 ms at 14:38**. [checkout-metrics:L126-L140] [checkout-metrics:L141-L160]
- At **14:19:19–14:19:36**, three logged requests each timed out on attempt **1/4** after **8002 ms**, with `next=retry` and `backoff_ms=250`. At 14:20–14:21 there are further 8000 ms timeouts; one request progresses to attempt **2/4**, then retries with **500 ms** backoff. [payment-client-log:L184-L186] [payment-client-log:L187-L191] [payment-client-log:L192-L200]
- The log search found **8** examples of attempt **4/4** timing out and giving up, between **14:26:00** and **15:00:58**. [payment-client-log:L222-L222] [payment-client-log:L237-L237] [payment-client-log:L312-L312] [payment-client-log:L320-L320] [payment-client-log:L380-L380] [payment-client-log:L398-L398] [payment-client-log:L446-L446] [payment-client-log:L481-L481]
- A sampled normal checkout trace at **14:19:00** lasted **412 ms**: cart load **22 ms**, address validation **22 ms**, fraud screen **56 ms**, payment authorization **288 ms** (one successful attempt), and order persistence **13 ms**. This is one normal trace, not a representative slow trace. [traces-2026-10-06:L310-L316]
- **DB/reindex competitor:** concurrent reindex ran **14:10–14:41**; change log expected elevated CPU, no table locks, and possibly slightly higher query latency. Orders-db CPU alert fired at **14:15** at **84%** (threshold 75%). [db-change-log:L7] [alerts-log:L5] Excerpted DB metric rows show the first value at **80–92** from 14:10–14:40 and **26** at 14:41; metric headers were not included in the excerpt, so interpret cautiously. [db-metrics:L132-L163]
- Provider reported EU-1 authorization impact around **14:18–15:05**, identified a faulty acquirer connection pool on some nodes at 14:51, drained affected nodes at 15:04, and marked the issue resolved at 15:09. [provider-status:L5-L9] Checkout alerts resolved at **15:06** and **15:07**; ticket says latency looked normal by **15:12**. [alerts-log:L9-L10] [ticket:L19-L20]

### Findings and hypotheses
- **Best supported:** EU-1 gateway degradation triggered the slowdown; v18’s longer timeout and greater retry allowance plausibly amplified the duration. Provider impact overlaps the sharp latency rise, and logs show repeated 8-second timeouts and retries during it. The p95 values around 17–34 seconds are consistent with multiple attempts, but the full per-request timing is not yet established. [provider-status:L5-L9] [payment-client-log:L184-L200] [payment-client-log:L222-L222] [checkout-metrics:L141-L160]
- **Main competitor—orders-db CPU/reindex:** plausible concurrent contributor: CPU was elevated during reindex and overlaps the incident. It is not ruled out; however, CPU returned to **26** at 14:41 while checkout remained slow afterward, and the sampled trace’s DB spans were short. [db-metrics:L132-L163] [checkout-metrics:L163-L180] [traces-2026-10-06:L311-L316]
- **Address validation:** sampled spans of **22–40 ms** are much shorter than multi-second delays, weakening (not fully excluding) this hypothesis. [traces-2026-10-06:L207-L242] [traces-2026-10-06:L333-L370]
- **Useful comparison:** Oct 4, on v2.13.3/profile 17, checkout p95 reached about **4.2 s** during a separate EU-1 authorization incident. This supports gateway sensitivity independent of v2.14.0, while Oct 6’s greater severity may reflect v18 amplification. [checkout-metrics:L34-L58] [alerts-log:L1-L4] [provider-status:L11-L14]

### Next steps / mitigation
1. Inspect representative **slow** traces and full payment-client log sequences to establish per-request attempt counts, elapsed durations, and contribution from retries; compare Oct 4 with Oct 6.
2. Read DB metric headers/full series and compare query latency/pool waits with checkout timing before concluding the DB explanation is ruled out.
3. If mitigation is warranted, the runbook’s smallest reversible option is a **runtime payment-client profile rollback to v17**, with incident commander approval; do not execute it as part of this read-only investigation. Preserve idempotency and fraud screening. Runbook calls for monitoring latency/error ratio for 15 minutes and checking reconciliation for duplicate charges. [runbook-payments:L3-L8] [runbook-payments:L12-L15] [runbook-payments:L19-L22]

5| 1. Fraud screening must run before every authorization. Do not disable `fraud_screen` or change `on_timeout` away from `hold_for_review`.

function.name: list_artifacts
function.description: List the artifacts in the incident evidence bundle with their ids, sizes and a short description.

function.name: search_artifacts
function.description: Find lines that contain ALL query terms (case-insensitive substring match; use "double quotes" for a phrase). Add in:<artifact-id> to restrict the search to one or more artifacts. Returns the total match count per artifact and at most 40 matching lines as <artifact-id>:L<line>| <text>.

function.name: read_artifact
function.description: Read lines of one artifact. offset is the 1-based line number of the first line (default 1); limit is a number of lines (default 100, max 200). A read returns at most 16000 characters; the header reports bounded_by and next_offset when more lines remain. Each line is prefixed with its line number.
